t: #2190 Most Frequent Number Following Key In an Array
o: We scan adjacent pairs `(nums[i], nums[i+1])` and, whenever `nums[i] == key`, credit `nums[i+1]` as a follower of key. The answer is the follower with the most credits. In Example 1, key=1 appears at indices 0 and 3, followed by 100 twice, so the answer is 100. In Example 2, key=2 appears at indices 0–2, followed by 2 three times and 3 once, so the answer is 2. Constraints are tiny (n ≤ 1000, values ≤ 1000), so any linear scan with a counter works.
k: Only the immediate successor of each occurrence of key matters — one linear pass suffices.
Values are bounded by 1000, so either a hash map or a fixed-size frequency array works.

a.i: Walk through the array once; every time `nums[i] == key`, increment a counter for `nums[i+1]`. Finally return the key with the maximum count. This directly mirrors the problem definition.
s: For each i from 0 to n-2, if nums[i] == key, increment count[nums[i+1]].
Return the map entry with the largest value.
a.t: O(n) — single pass plus a scan of the map.
a.sp: O(u) — u is the number of unique followers of key.

a.i: Since values lie in [1, 1000], replace the hash map with an array of size 1001 indexed by value. This removes hashing overhead and makes finding the max a simple array scan.
s: Scan freq for the index with the maximum count.
a.t: O(n + V) where V = 1000 — one pass plus a bounded scan.

w: Prefer the hash-map version in interviews for generality; mention the array version as an optimization given bounded values. Pitfalls: forgetting the pair constraint (only immediate successors count) and off-by-one on the loop bound (i goes to n-2). Follow-ups: what if 'follows within distance d'? Use a sliding window of the next d elements.
